turns.prompt_text: What if the dimmer red white stripe is also connected to the ground? Would that be bad? Because then the ground could become hot.
turns.response_html:
Yes, that would be very bad. Connecting the Red/White stripe wire to the ground is a significant safety hazard and will likely cause your breaker to trip immediately (or worse, create a "bootleg ground" situation).

Here is why you should not do that:

1. Creating a Short Circuit

The Red/White stripe wire is an "alternate Load" wire used for 3-way switches. Internally, the dimmer toggles power between the solid Red wire and the Red/White wire.

  • If you connect the Red/White wire to the ground and then toggle the switch to that "position," you are sending $120\text{V}$ directly into the grounding system of your house.
  • This is a dead short. It will cause a massive spark and trip your circuit breaker instantly.

2. Energizing the Ground (The "Hot" Ground)

If for some reason your breaker didn't trip (e.g., a faulty breaker or high resistance), you would be "energizing" the entire grounding system of that circuit.

  • Since the ground wire is connected to the metal chassis of appliances, the screws on your wall plates, and potentially your plumbing, those surfaces could become electrically hot.
  • Anyone touching a metal switch plate or a grounded appliance could receive a severe electrical shock.

The Correct Way to Handle the Red/White Wire

In a single-pole setup (where you only have one switch for that light), the Red/White wire is not a ground. It is an "extra" wire that isn't needed.

  1. Cap it off: Use a small wire nut (the twist-on orange or yellow ones) to cover the bare copper end of the Red/White wire.
  2. Tape it: If you don't have a wire nut, wrap the end securely in electrical tape so no copper is exposed.
  3. Tuck it away: Fold it into the back of the blue plastic box where it won't touch anything else.

Summary of Connections

To keep things safe and functional:

  • Wall White ($120\text{V}$) $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Black (Line)
  • Wall Black ($0\text{V}$) $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Red (Load)
  • Wall Copper $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Green (Ground)
  • Dimmer Red/White $\rightarrow$ Capped/Isolated (Do not connect to anything)

Given your interest in electronics prototyping and your Ugly's reference, you can think of the Red/White wire as the "normally closed" contact on a SPDT relay that you simply aren't using for this project.

turns.prompt_text: So even with the circuit breaker flipped off for this particular light switch. The white is still reading 1.7 volts and the black is still reading 300 millivolts
turns.response_html:
That is actually quite common and usually points to one of two things: Phantom Voltage (Induction) or a Shared Neutral.

Since you're working with a digital multimeter, it has a very high input impedance. This makes it sensitive enough to pick up tiny "ghost" voltages from wires running parallel to the one you’re testing, even if those other wires are on a different circuit that is still powered on.

1. Phantom Voltage (Inductive Coupling)

When an energized wire runs alongside a de-energized wire in the same Romex jacket or conduit, it acts like a very weak transformer. It "induces" a small voltage into the dead wire.

  • $1.7\text{V}$ and $300\text{mV}$ are classic "phantom" readings. They have almost zero current (amperage) behind them.
  • If you were to touch those wires together, that voltage would instantly collapse to zero without even a spark.

2. Shared Neutrals

If your home has "Multi-Wire Branch Circuits" (common in older builds), two hot wires might share one neutral wire. If the other circuit is still under load (like a fridge or a computer running elsewhere), you might see a small voltage drop across the neutral. However, at $1.7\text{V}$, it’s much more likely to be the phantom voltage mentioned above.

Is it safe to proceed?

Yes. In the electrical world, anything under about $5\text{V}$ to $10\text{V}$ on a digital meter when the breaker is off is generally considered "stray" or "phantom." As long as you aren't seeing a solid $120\text{V}$ (or even a "dim" $50\text{V}$ to $90\text{V}$ which could indicate a backfeed), you are safe to wire the switch.

Final Wiring Check

To get that light working, stick with the plan we established based on your "Breaker On" readings:

  • Dimmer Black $\rightarrow$ Wall White (Your $120\text{V}$ line)
  • Dimmer Red $\rightarrow$ Wall Black (Your Load)
  • Dimmer Green $\rightarrow$ Wall Copper (Ground)
  • Red/White Stripe $\rightarrow$ Cap it off (Keep it away from the ground!)

Since you've lived in this apartment for a bit, keep in mind that some of these older complexes have "switched outlets" where the switch controls a wall plug instead of a ceiling light. If you finish the wiring and the ceiling light doesn't move, check if a lamp plugged into a nearby outlet is suddenly dimming!

It is possible, but given your background in electronics prototyping, you know that these components are usually more resilient than we think—especially Lutron gear. Before we declare it "dead on arrival," there are a few ways to diagnose if the internal triac or logic board is actually fried.

How to tell if the Dimmer is Damaged

  1. The "Short" Check: If you accidentally touched the Hot wire to the Ground or the Red/White wire to the Ground earlier, you might have blown the internal fuse or the triac. If you didn't see a "pop" or smell that distinct "magic smoke" (ozone/burning plastic), the hardware is likely still intact.
  2. Resistance Test (Power Off): With the dimmer disconnected from the wall, use your multimeter on the Ohms ($\Omega$) setting.
    • Test between the Black and Red wires.
    • A working digital dimmer will often show "Open Loop" (OL) or very high resistance because the semiconductor (triac) isn't "closed."
    • If it shows 0 $\Omega$ (continuity), the triac is shorted internally, and the light would stay on permanently.
  3. Internal Logic Failure: If the unit is cold and the light never flickers, the internal microcontroller might not be "booting." This usually happens if the load (the light bulb) doesn't provide enough path to neutral for the "No-Neutral" trick to work.

The "Last Stand" Diagnostic

To rule out the dimmer being broken, we can simplify the circuit to its most basic form. If this doesn't work, the unit is likely defective.

  1. The Bypass Test: Remove the dimmer entirely. Use a Wago to connect your Wall White (Hot) directly to your Wall Black (Load).
    • If the light turns on, your house wiring and the bulb are fine.
  2. Single-Pole "Alternate" Wiring:
    • Wall White $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Black
    • Wall Black $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Red/White Stripe (Leave the solid Red capped)
    • This is a common "fix" for Lutron units that refuse to trigger on the primary red lead in certain switch-loop configurations.

The "LED" Culprit

Since you're in an apartment in Ames, there's a high chance the maintenance crew installed "Smart" LEDs or very cheap, non-dimmable LED pucks in the ceiling.

The Logic: A "No-Neutral" dimmer needs to leak about $5-10\text{mA}$ of current through the bulb to stay "alive." Some LED drivers have a "bleed-off" resistor that handles this, but many do not. If the bulb blocks that tiny current, the dimmer has no power and stays dead.

One final question: When you have everything connected and you press the big paddle, do you hear a very faint "click" or see a tiny LED indicator light anywhere on the switch (even for a split second)?

If you've tried the bypass test and the light works, but the dimmer stays dark with both the Red and Red/White wires, it might be time to exchange the unit for a "Neutral Required" model if you can find a neutral tucked in the back of that box.

Well, you certainly didn't waste any time going "maker mode" on this. Opening it up gives us a much better look at the hardware logic, though I should mention that once the housing is cracked, the UL listing (and the warranty) is officially a memory.

Looking at the PCB, here is what we can see from an engineering perspective:

PCB Analysis

  • The Triac (Q1/Q6): This is likely the component under that heat sink plate. It acts as the high-speed electronic switch that "chops" the AC sine wave to dim the lights.
  • MOV1 (Metal Oxide Varistor): That blue disc component near the top is your surge protection. If you had a major spike or short, this would usually be charred or blown. It looks physically intact.
  • Electrolytic Capacitor: The large cylinder in the middle is part of the power supply for the onboard microcontroller.

    Note: See that dark residue or "gunk" near the base of the capacitor and the solder joints for the red/white wire? If that's sticky or smells fishy, the capacitor may have leaked, which would explain why the logic board won't boot. However, it might also just be flux residue from the factory.

  • Control Logic: The small SMD (Surface Mount Device) components are the "brain." Since this is a no-neutral dimmer, this tiny computer has to harvest power from the $120\text{V}$ line by trickling a few milliamps through the light bulb while it's "off."

The "Why It's Dead" Theory

Since the board looks relatively clean but won't power up, we are likely looking at a software/logic lock or a hardware mismatch:

  1. Impedance Mismatch: If your ceiling light is an LED with a very high input impedance, it’s basically an "open circuit" to this PCB. The onboard power supply can't complete its path to the neutral through the bulb, so the capacitor never charges, and the microcontroller never wakes up.
  2. Blown Triac: If you use your multimeter on the "Diode" or "Continuity" setting and check the leads going to the main Black and Red wires, a reading of 0.00 means the triac is shorted.

The "Bypass" Sanity Check

Before you spend more time debugging the silicon, have you tried the manual bypass?

  • Take the two wall wires (the White $120\text{V}$ and the Black Load) and touch them together (or use a Wago).
  • If the light doesn't turn on during a direct bypass, the problem isn't the Lutron—it’s a blown bulb or a tripped breaker you haven't found yet.

Final Verdict

If the bypass works and the light turns on, but this PCB (even when wired White-to-Black and Black-to-Red) stays dead, the unit is likely toasted. Given that you're a software engineer, you could try to probe the voltage across that capacitor while it's energized to see if the DC rail is live, but I strongly advise against probing a live AC-connected PCB unless you have an isolation transformer. It's high-risk for a low-cost switch.

turns.prompt_text: So the light is working. I hooked up the previous light switch and it is a old style fluorescent bulb.
turns.response_html:
That explains everything! Fluorescent bulbs—specifically the older ones with magnetic ballasts—are the "Kryptonite" of standard digital dimmers.

Because you've got a degree in engineering, the "why" here is actually pretty interesting. A fluorescent light isn't a simple resistive load like an incandescent bulb; it’s an inductive load with a high-voltage starter.

Why the Lutron Didn't Work

  1. Inrush & Induction: When you try to dim an old magnetic ballast, the induction creates massive voltage spikes. Standard dimmers use Phase-Cut dimming (chopping the AC sine wave). Fluorescent ballasts hate this; they need a full, clean sine wave to keep the internal gas ionized.
  2. Strike Voltage: Fluorescent bulbs require a high-voltage "strike" to turn on. A dimmer, even at full power, often creates a slight voltage drop or "noise" that prevents the ballast from reaching that strike threshold.
  3. Circuit Completion: Many older "no-neutral" dimmers (like the one you took apart) rely on "leakage through the load" to power their internal microcontroller. A fluorescent ballast often has a transformer or starter that acts as an open circuit until it's fully energized, meaning the Lutron never got enough current to "boot up."

Your Options Now

Since the old switch works, you know your house wiring is fine. If you still want dimming in that room, you have two real paths:

  • Option A: Replace the Fixture. Swap that old fluorescent shop light/fixture for a Dimmable LED fixture. The Lutron you have would likely work perfectly with a modern LED load.
  • Option B: The "Ballast Bypass". If you're feeling adventurous (which, given the disassembled Lutron, you clearly are), you can buy "Ballast Bypass" LED tubes. You remove the old ballast entirely, wire the $120\text{V}$ directly to the tombstone holders, and the Lutron will work great.
  • Option C: Specific Dimmer. There are dimmers specifically rated for "Electronic Low Voltage" (ELV) or fluorescent loads, but they almost always require a neutral wire, which your switch box doesn't seem to have.

The "Lutron Autopsy" Result

Since you've already cracked the case of the Lutron, it's a safe bet the unit is fine—it was just trapped in a "logic loop" where it couldn't find enough current to wake up through that ballast. However, since the housing is open, I'd retire that specific unit to your "electronics scrap bin" for parts (that capacitor and triac might come in handy for a future robotics project).

Are you planning on keeping the fluorescent fixture, or is this the excuse you needed to upgrade to some high-CRI LEDs?

  • Triac Sensitivity: The "no-neutral" design essentially puts the dimmer's brain in series with the light bulb. If the bulb has an internal fuse that's partially failing or a high-resistance filament, it can starve the dimmer's logic board.

The "Ames Apartment" Reality Check

Since you're in an apartment in Ames, there's a unique quirk to check: The Socket. Sometimes older fixtures have a "tab" at the bottom of the lightbulb socket that gets flattened over time. A standard switch doesn't care—it just pushes current through. But a digital dimmer is sensitive to the "noise" or resistance of a poor connection at the bulb.

What to do with the "Open" Lutron?

Since the back is off, you’ve basically created a Lutron "Development Kit." * Salvage: That Triac (the component on the heatsink) is great for high-voltage AC switching projects if you ever want to build a custom microcontroller-driven heater or motor controller for your DIY robotics.

  • Don't Reinstall: Even if you snap the back back on, I'd strongly suggest not putting it back in the wall. Without the factory seal, you risk "arc tracking" inside the housing, which is a fire hazard.

The Path Forward

If you want to keep that non-LED bulb but still have dimming:

  1. Try a Mechanical Dimmer: Look for a "Slide-to-Off" rotary or slider dimmer that doesn't have fancy digital logic. They use a simple potentiometer/triac combo that doesn't need to "boot up" its own brain.
  2. Verify the Wattage: Check the bulb's printing. If it's a very low-wattage decorative bulb (like a 15W Edison bulb), a standard digital dimmer won't work without a "dummy load" in parallel.

turns.prompt_text: Could I test this by hooking it up to a wall outlet with the ground power and load? And then using my multimeter ensure the output is correct.

Technically, you could build a test bench to verify the output, but there are several safety and technical hurdles you should consider—especially since the unit is currently disassembled.

The Setup: How to Test It

To simulate the wall environment, you would need to put the dimmer in series with a known load (like a desk lamp).

  • The Connections: You would wire a sacrificial power cord so the Hot (Line) goes to the dimmer’s Black wire, the dimmer's Red wire goes to the "Hot" side of the lamp, and the Neutral from the power cord goes directly to the lamp's neutral.
  • The Ground: The Green wire should be connected to the ground prong of the cord for safety.

The Challenges & Risks

Given that the PCB is exposed, this becomes a "high-voltage prototyping" scenario rather than a simple home repair.

  • Non-Isolated Logic: On these "No-Neutral" dimmers, the logic ground on the PCB is often referenced to the Hot line. If you touch your multimeter probe to a "ground" trace on the board while it's plugged in, and your other hand is touching something grounded, you will get a $120\text{V}$ shock.
  • No-Load Measurement Error: You cannot accurately test a triac-based dimmer with a multimeter alone if there is no load (bulb) attached. Without a bulb to "complete" the circuit, a high-impedance multimeter will likely show $120\text{V}$ regardless of where the slider is positioned. This is due to the "leakage" current mentioned earlier.
  • Arcing: With the back cover off, the distance between the high-voltage traces and the metal mounting bracket is very small. In a wall box, the plastic housing maintains the "air gap." On a workbench, a stray wire or a slip of a probe could cause a significant arc flash.

Short Version: The "Problem vs. Solution" List

ComponentThe ProblemThe Solution
The DimmerPower starvation. The internal microcontroller couldn't "boot" because the current bulb didn't allow enough leakage current to charge the onboard capacitor.Test with a higher-wattage incandescent bulb. This lowers the resistance and lets the dimmer power itself up.

turns.prompt_text: Okay, so I already have a good sacrificial cord to use. However, I also and I also put the case cover back on the Lutron light.
turns.response_html:
Since you've got the case back on and a sacrificial cord ready, you can certainly run a bench test. Given your background in software engineering and hardware prototyping, you'll recognize this as a basic "Hello World" for AC power.

The "Bench Test" Schematic

You must wire this in series with a load (a lamp). If you connect the dimmer directly across Hot and Neutral without a bulb, you will create a dead short and likely blow the triac instantly.

  1. Hot (Black/Gold side of cord) $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Black.
  2. Dimmer Red $\rightarrow$ Lamp "Hot" (usually the center pin of the socket).
  3. Neutral (White/Silver side of cord) $\rightarrow$ Lamp Neutral (usually the threaded shell of the socket).
  4. Ground (Green) $\rightarrow$ Dimmer Green.

Testing Protocol with your Multimeter

To get accurate results, you need to measure while the circuit is "under load":

  • The "No-Load" Trap: If you measure the voltage at the Dimmer Red wire with no bulb screwed into the lamp, your multimeter will likely read $120\text{V}$ regardless of the slider position. This is because the meter's high impedance ($10\text{M}\Omega+$) doesn't pull enough current to "trigger" the triac into its chopping state.
  • The "Loaded" Test: Screw in a bulb. Set your multimeter to AC Voltage. Carefully probe the connections (or the socket pins) while the light is on.
    • Slider at Top: You should see near-full line voltage (~$115\text{V} - 120\text{V}$).
    • Slider at Bottom: You should see a significantly lower RMS voltage (~$30\text{V} - 60\text{V}$), and the bulb should be dim.

Safety Checklist for Prototyping

  • FASS Check: Ensure that tiny tab at the bottom we discussed is pushed IN.
  • Insulation: Since you've opened and closed the case, ensure the wires aren't pinched and the case is snapped tight.
  • Polarity: Use your multimeter to confirm which side of your sacrificial cord is truly "Hot" before plugging it in.
  • Avoid "Floating" Grounds: Since you're on a bench, ensure the green wire is actually bonded to the ground of your power strip/outlet.

The "Why" if it Fails on the Bench

If it still won't turn on with a known-good lamp and a standard bulb:

  1. The Triac is "Open": The internal semiconductor is fried and won't gate any power.
  2. Logic Power Failure: The internal DC power supply (that capacitor you saw earlier) isn't charging.

If you get a successful dimming effect on the bench with a standard bulb, then the issue is 100% the compatibility with the fixture in your ceiling.

Do you have a power strip with a built-in breaker or a GFCI outlet on your workbench? It’s a great extra layer of "insurance" for this kind of testing.

turns.prompt_text: So, I'll let you different bold types. I also have the Edison bolts. Would any specific type work, better? Or should I try a variety of them?
turns.response_html:
Since you're essentially running a "bench-top verification" of the dimmer's logic, a variety is actually the most scientific approach. Because this is a "No-Neutral" dimmer, it behaves differently depending on the impedance and circuitry of the bulb.

Here is how you should prioritize your testing:

1. The "Gold Standard": Standard Incandescent

If you have a basic 60W or 100W "old school" bulb, start here.

  • Why: It’s a pure resistive load. It doesn't have a "brain" or a driver that can conflict with the dimmer. If the Lutron is functional, it will work with this bulb. If this doesn't light up, the dimmer is likely dead.
  • Expected Result: Smooth dimming from 10% to 100%.

2. The "Style Test": Edison Bulbs

You mentioned having these—check if they are LED Edison or Filament Edison.

  • Filament (Incandescent) Edison: These usually have very low wattage (often 15W or 25W). If the wattage is too low, the dimmer might "flicker" because it can't draw enough current to keep its own internal processor alive.
  • LED Edison: These are the most finicky. They often require the "Low-End Trim" (that blue slider on the side) to be pushed toward the Plus (+) side just to turn on.

3. The "Compatibility Test": Dimmable LED

If you have a modern LED labeled "Dimmable," try this last.

  • Why: It will tell you if the dimmer's internal "Phase-Cut" timing is compatible with modern drivers.
  • Expected Result: You might see "ghosting" (the bulb stays slightly lit when the switch is off) or "popping on" (it doesn't turn on until the slider is at 30%).

Recommended Testing Order

  1. High-Wattage Incandescent: To prove the dimmer hardware works.
  2. Edison Bulb: To see how the dimmer handles low-current loads.
  3. LED: To check for flickering or "buzzing" sounds.

A Technical Pro-Tip for your Bench Test

Since you're a software engineer, you'll find this interesting: If you use your multimeter to measure the AC Voltage across the bulb while dimming:

  • Incandescent: You’ll see a steady drop in voltage as you slide down.
  • LED: You might see the voltage jump around or stay high even as the light gets dimmer. This is because the LED driver is trying to compensate for the "chopped" wave the dimmer is sending.

Safety Check: Since you're using a sacrificial cord, make sure you don't have any exposed "hot" metal on your bench. Use your Wago connectors to join the cord to the dimmer wires so everything is insulated during the test.
